title: Why Kangaroos Hop 50 km/h Without Getting Tired 🦘
description:
Why do kangaroos hop instead of run? Their huge Achilles tendons stretch like springs on every landing and snap back to launch the next hop, so a red kangaroo's oxygen use barely rises as it hops faster, and each bounce even pumps air in and out of its lungs.

topic: Why do kangaroos hop instead of run?
script: How do kangaroos hit 50 kilometres an hour with almost no extra energy, when you'd be gasping? As a red kangaroo hops faster, its oxygen use barely changes. So why hop instead of run? It's all in the legs. Each one has a huge Achilles tendon, and it works like a pogo spring. When the kangaroo lands, the tendon stretches, storing energy. Then it snaps back and launches the next hop. One bound can cover up to nine metres. And there's a bonus. Every bounce sloshes its gut up and down, which pumps air in and out of its lungs. So hopping helps it breathe too. Going slow is the clumsy part. Then it walks on five legs, using its tail as the fifth. So if you had pogo-spring legs, would you ever walk again?
key_facts: As red kangaroos hop faster, their rate of oxygen consumption remains nearly the same (Kram & Dawson 1998, PubMed 9787777)
Long springy Achilles tendons stretch on landing and recoil to launch the next hop (Discover Wildlife; eLife/EurekAlert 2025)
Red kangaroos can reach roughly 56-70 km/h in short bursts and cover up to about 9 m in a single hop (Discover Wildlife)
The hopping motion drives the gut up and down, inflating and deflating the lungs (Discover Wildlife)
At slow speeds kangaroos use a pentapedal gait with forelimbs, hindlimbs and tail on the ground (eLife/EurekAlert)
